problem: Training-based ObjNav models (foundation models, diffusion policies) need huge data and compute and generalize poorly to diverse object categories, while training-free egocentric or frontier-based VLM methods revisit explored areas or travel back and forth between distant frontiers, giving low SPL.
motivation: ObjNav efficiency (how directly the agent explores) matters as much as success, since it determines how much time remains for later tasks. The authors argue that egocentric VLM selection lacks global context and that frontier methods lack a global spatial-reasonableness check, so combining both views with depth should give more efficient exploration without training.
key_idea: A training-free, depth-aware VLM framework: depth-thresholded ego-view region candidates are chosen by a VLM (VQA), then verified on the top-down map by a second VLM query, with history-based pruning and a nearest-frontier fallback.
insight: Efficiency comes from combining local (egocentric) selection with a global top-down check plus pruning of already-explored regions, which reduces frontier-to-frontier back-and-forth. Evidence is mostly indirect: the real-world comparison against nearest-frontier exploration (5 episodes) shows similar SR but much higher SPL/EoS (0.65 vs 0.43 SPL, 0.81 vs 0.72 EoS). There is no proper simulation ablation of the modules. Failure analysis shows HM3D failures are mostly navigation-related (Constraint Map ~45%), while OVON failures are mostly semantic/detection errors.
method: Ego Region Selecting (Module a): thresholds depth (e.g. >5 m) to create candidate region masks, labels them with numeric IDs on the RGB view, and asks Qwen2.5-VL-7B via VQA which region best leads to the goal.

Global-wise Checking (Module b): projects the chosen region onto the top-down map, colors it, and asks the same VLM whether it is a good option; if rejected, falls back to the next-best candidate. History-aware pruning removes candidates beyond a set margin from the explored-area boundary.
Frontier fallback: if all candidates are rejected, the nearest frontier pixel on the explored-area boundary is used as the target (rarely invoked).

Destination Confirmation and Path Planning (Modules c/d): picks the nearest candidate area (dilating the mask if unreachable), then plans with A* on a dilated-obstacle map with replanning, executed as discrete turn/forward actions.
Map construction: initial 360° rotation, then incremental top-down map from depth and odometry.

Finalization: Qwen2.5-VL detects the goal, MobileSAM segments it, and the mask plus depth is projected as the goal region. The goal is refreshed every 5 steps, and termination is by pixel distance to the goal region.

Memory extension for GOAT-Bench: stores previously found object locations and navigates directly to them when they are requested again, otherwise runs standard ObjNav. Also proposes the EoS metric = SPL/SR.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-7B (frozen) for decisions and detection, MobileSAM for segmentation
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: turn left/right 30°, move forward 2.5 m, terminate (A* path following)
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D, OVON, GOAT-Bench); real Unitree Go2 robot

numbers_note: HM3D is the 'val' split per the text (2019 episodes); it was mapped to 'val' as printed. The paper reports an inconsistent mean EoS in the text (66.33, CV 0.085) versus the table (66.79, CV 0.083). Real-world results are only 5 episodes per method (EffiNav SR 0.80, SPL 0.65, EoS 0.81 vs nearest frontier 0.60/0.43/0.72) and are not counted as a benchmark.
results: EffiNav (training-free, Qwen2.5-VL-7B) gets SR 55.0 / SPL 36.7 on HM3D, second to UniNavid (73.7 / 37.1), which needs 483k training samples and ~1400 GPU-hours. On OVON it gets SR 63.0 / SPL 43.7, beating UniNavid (39.5 / 19.8) and NavFom (43.6 / 31.3). On GOAT-Bench it reaches SR 52.3 / SPL 48.5 versus 3D-Mem's 49.6 / 29.4.
limitations: Relies on accurate depth; estimated depth (Depth Anything 3) was unreliable, and real sensors fail on some materials, producing incomplete maps.
Ego and top-down inputs are 2D images that lose spatial information; final goal detection is a 2D detector sensitive to viewpoint; SR on HM3D (55.0) is well below the best trained model.
No module-level ablations in simulation; real-world validation is tiny (5 episodes, one goal), and the EoS metric is just SPL/SR.
